job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Dana Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake at seven, take the bus to Hartley Furniture Supply, and spend the day in accounts payable: matching supplier invoices to purchase orders, chasing missing paperwork, entering totals. I studied business administration at the state university and passed, with no internships, so this job felt lucky. I share a flat with two girls, and I go to my aunt Rosa's most Sundays for a proper meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, because most of the tools my firm bought last year just made the same work a bit slower to learn. At work we'd carry on matching invoices to purchase orders like always. Online I'd probably not say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I've only been in the accounts payable office at Hartley Furniture Supply for four months, and I'm still learning where everything goes. If the pace stays the same, I can learn it properly and nobody rushes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to work, pay my share of the rent in the flat I share with two others, and put about 150 a month toward my student loan. I'd also keep going to the union meetings that my aunt Rosa, who works at the hospital, drags me to. I'd stay away from the new software unless my manager makes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. I still worry a bit about money because my loan statement arrives every month and it hasn't got smaller yet, but my job feels normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from the software. What would you do if your manager made you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You asked what would change at work. Nothing big, but there's one thing: Colin, my team lead, keeps talking about an auto-matching tool for invoices. If it saved time he might not need a second junior, so I do wonder about that. Even a little tool could matter for a team of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the company would really retrain you, or is that hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool took my invoice matching, I'd ask to be moved to supplier queries, which is the part where you talk to real people. I'd rather the company retrain me than hire someone new. A fair company does that, and I'd say so out loud.

say: I'd say **nothing much** has changed, and the tools we've bought only added training time.
I'd tell friends it's mostly **hype**, but I'd keep an eye on my team.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, because a slow pace lets me learn the job properly.
I do worry that one small matching tool could mean the company **never hires** another junior.
do: Keep paying **150 a month** toward my student loan and stay in the shared flat.
Go to the **union meetings** with my aunt Rosa and ask about retraining rights.
feel: I feel **steady**, with a small knot about the loan statement.
S0.quote: Even a little tool could matter for a team of four.
fieldNote: Dana is cautious and likes the **familiar**, so a slow world suits her.
Her worry is specific: one small tool could remove the next junior hire on a team of four.

steps.text: Pay 150 a month toward the student loan
Go to union meetings with aunt Rosa each month
Ask Colin about moving to supplier queries if matching is automated

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company is going to use this as an excuse to hire fewer people and call it progress. At work I'd keep it polite, but with my friends I'd say workers need a say before the tools arrive. Online I'd probably share articles about unions bargaining over AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, my job is exactly the type that goes first. Matching invoices, checking totals and chasing missing paperwork is what AI does best. I'm two years into paying a loan and I haven't even finished my probation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd build a bit more cushion, so maybe 400 a month saved instead of 150, even if it means no holidays. I'd ask the union rep at Hartley about what the contract says on redundancy. I'd also finally sit with Colin and learn the checking software, even though I really don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach tight. Picture a ladder being pulled up right when I'm putting my foot on the first rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you dislike the checking software. What changes your mind about learning it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, Elena, cooks at a primary school, and she'd say find something with people in it. She can lend me a few hundred in a bad month, but not more. I'd tell her I'm trying, and I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones I'd worry about are the new starters after me, because I think the company will just stop hiring juniors. Whoever is already in gets squeezed, but at least has a job. It's the people still looking who get hit hardest.

say: I'd say firms will use this to **hire fewer** people, and workers deserve a say.
I'd share union articles online but stay **polite** at work.
think: My job is mostly matching and checking, which is exactly what AI does **first**.
I'm worried the company will simply **stop hiring** juniors, and I'm still on probation.
do: Raise monthly savings from 150 to **400**, giving up holidays.
Ask the **union rep** at Hartley what the contract says about redundancy.
Sit with Colin and **learn** the checking software, reluctantly.
feel: My stomach feels **tight**, like the ladder is being pulled up as I step on it.
S1.quote: Picture a ladder being pulled up right when I'm putting my foot on the first rung.
fieldNote: Dana **blames** employers and wants rules and union voice before the tools arrive.
She is reluctant on tools but will learn one to protect herself, which shows how real the pressure is.

steps.text: Ask the Hartley union rep about redundancy terms
Learn the invoice checking software with Colin
Ask mum Elena what help she can give in a bad month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is something governments should have stopped and prepared for, and two years is a joke. I'd be loud about it online, and I'd want unions and politicians in the room before any firm switches people off. At work I'd probably go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone within a year or so. Accounts payable is all rules and documents. The firm has no reason to keep four of us when one person and a program can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut everything: no eating out, cancel the streaming, move into the smaller room in the flat for 120 less. I'd go to the union and push for severance rules. I'd also join the protest the union organises outside the town hall, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor has gone. I'd be lying awake doing sums on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd have no time to retrain properly. I owe 14,000, and my mum can only lend a little. If I lose the job in the first year I'd move back in with my mum in Eastfield and apply for whatever help exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're angry. Who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm more angry than scared, if I'm honest. Someone decided to build this at speed and nobody in my position was asked. I'd say that straight to anyone who'd listen, and I'd vote for whoever promised support.

say: I'd say **two years** is a joke and governments should have prepared.
I'd push for **unions** and politicians to act before firms switch people off.
think: I think my job in accounts payable is **gone** within a year.
I'm **angrier** than scared, because nobody like me was asked.
do: Cut spending hard, including the **smaller room** at 120 less a month.
Join the union **protest** and push for severance rules.
Move back to my mum's in **Eastfield** if the job goes.
feel: It feels like the **floor** has gone, and I'd lie awake doing sums.
S2.quote: Someone decided to build this at speed and nobody in my position was asked.
fieldNote: Dana's **anger** points at governments and firms who decided at speed, not at the technology.
With 14,000 debt and little time, she expects a real loss of income in the first year.

steps.text: Move to the smaller room and save 120 a month
Join the union protest outside the town hall
Apply for state help if the job goes
Move back to mum's in Eastfield if laid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but at least a person could plan something. At work I'd ask the union to push for a deal on retraining. Online, I'd back anyone calling for public support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the entry-level desk job I have now won't exist by then, but I might still be in some job if I move early. I'd have my loan nearly down by 2031 if I kept paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd pay the loan down faster, aiming to cut it from 14,000 to about 8,000 over three years. I'd start an evening course in something people do, maybe payroll with a human side, or supplier relations. I'd keep my union membership and vote for the party that promises training grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less awful than two years. Five years feels like a storm warning rather than a bomb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you dislike change. How would that show up in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is I'm the type who dislikes change. I'd force myself to try the tools by year three, but only after other people showed it was safe. That's how I am, and it would cost me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually move to a different kind of job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job in a hospital or a school, where a person is the point, looks safer to me. My mum is a school cook and my aunt works at the hospital, and neither has been talking about robots. I'd think about that kind of work in year two or three.

say: I'd say **five years** is short but long enough to plan something.
I'd ask the union to push for **retraining** deals.
think: The entry-level desk job I have won't exist by then, but I might survive by **moving early**.
My dislike of change could **cost me**, and I know it.
do: Pay the loan down from 14,000 to about **8,000** over three years.
Start an **evening course** in payroll or supplier relations.
Look at **hospital or school** admin work by year three.
feel: It feels like a **storm warning** rather than a bomb.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a storm warning rather than a bomb.
fieldNote: Dana's **resistance** to change is something she names herself, and the warning time softens it.
She looks to people-facing jobs in public services like her mum and aunt have.

steps.text: Pay the student loan down to about 8,000
Take an evening course in payroll or supplier relations
Apply for hospital or school admin jobs in year three
Vote for the party promising training grants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough that I'd mostly say life carries on, and people should use the time to get ready. I'd tell friends to get a skill that needs a person in the room. Online I'd still push for rules, because ten years goes fast for governments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be fairly okay. I'd be 32, with the loan paid off, and I'd have time to change. I'd worry more for the people who don't plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for now and pay the loan down on schedule. By 25 I'd start a part-time course, maybe in HR or social work, something that needs people. I'd also keep volunteering with the union and maybe run for a rep position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though not carefree. Ten years is long enough to make a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently at 25 than you'd do at 22?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everything turned out fine I'd have wasted nothing, because a course in HR is useful anyway. I'd rather prepare for a storm that doesn't come than be caught by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the ten years turns out to be five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would help most is a public scheme that pays for retraining, run by people who know the work. I'd lobby for that through the union, and vote for it. Waiting for the company to look after us is not a plan.

say: I'd tell friends to get a skill that **needs a person** in the room.
I'd keep pushing for **rules**, since ten years goes fast for governments.
think: I'd be fairly **okay**: 32, loan paid off, and time to change.
I'd worry more about people who **don't plan** than about myself.
do: Keep the job and pay the loan **on schedule**.
Start a part-time **HR or social work** course by 25.
Run for a **union rep** role at Hartley.
feel: I feel **calmer**, not carefree, because I like having a plan.
S4.quote: I'd rather prepare for a storm that doesn't come than be caught by one.
fieldNote: Dana turns the **longer horizon** into a plan, with people-facing work as her fallback.
She trusts collective routes, such as the union and public schemes, more than company goodwill.

steps.text: Keep the Hartley job and pay the loan on schedule
Start a part-time HR or social work course by 25
Run for union rep at Hartley

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because I'd have no time and a 14,000 debt. What would help is a government scheme that pays people to retrain, plus a union deal at work so the company can't just drop us. I'd also want a clear notice period.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just add that nobody asks people at the bottom what they think. Young workers like me are the ones the tools hit first, and we've the least say. A sit-down with real workers would help.

headlineQuote: Waiting for the company to look after us is not a plan.
portrait: Dana is a business administration graduate, four months into an accounts payable job at a furniture wholesaler, **renting** a shared flat.
She is cautious and dislikes new tools, and she blames employers and governments rather than the technology itself.
Her moods rise from uneasy to **alarmed** as warning time shrinks, and she answers with savings, the union and people-facing work.
Her debt of about 14,000 and a mother who can only lend a little shape every decision.
biggestWorry: The **2028** warning worries her most: little time, **14,000** of debt and a job built on checking paperwork.
whatWouldHelp: A public **retraining** scheme, a union deal at work and a clear notice period if jobs go.
